To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
simulated herbivore attacks in the seedling phase of Nicotiana plants led to a reduction of root growth rates that was transient in nature.
simulated herbivore damage to Nicotiana attenuate seedlings led to transiently reduced root growth rates.

simulated herbivory leads to a transient decrease of growth rates of N. attenuata seedlings and that the application of the oral secretion or of MeJA to the leaves leads to a more pronounced decrease of growth rates.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of whether the root growth reduction observed in seedlings following simulated herbivory is a direct result of increased resource investment in defence, or whether it is a direct result from the wound response itself.
the question of how plants react to herbivory on a short-term scale.

a novel aspect of growth-defence trade-off, i.e. the transient reduction of root growth following herbivore attack, and it provides a mechanistic explanation for the growth reduction observed in the literature.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the growth reduction in Nicotiana is caused by a transient diversion of resources from root growth to leaf defence.
the growth of Nicotiana seedlings is negatively affected by the induction of a wound response.

root growth is negatively affected by herbivore attack in the seedling phase of N. attenuata, but that the magnitude of this reaction is dependent on the type of elicitor applied and the time point of measurement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the root growth reduction following simulated herbivory is a consequence of an increased allocation of carbon to the production of secondary metabolites.
the growth of Nicotiana seedlings is negatively affected by the simulated attack of Manduca, which can be explained by the diversion of resources into defence-related processes.
the root growth of Nicotiana plants is negatively affected by simulated herbivy, and that this effect is most likely caused by the endogenous production of jasmonic acid (JA).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the short-term growth response to a simulated herbivore damage can be quantitatively measured, which allows for the mechanistic dissection of resource trade-offs in growth and defence.
growth-defence trade-off mechanisms are already active in the seedling phase, and that they may have profound implications on seedling establishment and plant fitness.

root growth reactions to simulated herbivore damage can be detected within hours, which makes root growth a suitable proxy for the assessment of the impact of herbivory on plant growth dynamics in the field.
